Volhynia
vol-HIN-ee-a
n. (the Ruthenian province of the commonwealth, seat of Ostrog, where the first complete printed Slavonic Bible was produced in 1581)
Latin Volhynia, from the old town of Volyn on the Bug; Polish Wołyń, Ukrainian Volyn.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Volhynia is the province in which a great Orthodox magnate did for his own church what the Reformation was doing in the West, and where the same liberty produced the sharpest denial of Christ in Europe. Prince Konstanty Wasyl Ostrogski, the richest man in the commonwealth, founded at Ostrog about 1576 a school with Greek and Latin, gathered scholars, set up a press, and in 1581 printed the Ostrog Bible, the first complete Bible in Church Slavonic ever to be printed, collated from Greek and Slavonic manuscripts and furnished with prefaces. He refused the Union of Brest and died Orthodox. At the same time Volhynia, under the religious liberty of the Warsaw Confederation of 1573, filled with congregations of the Polish Brethren, the antitrinitarian body which denied the deity of the Son and the satisfaction of the cross, sheltered by Reformed and Orthodox nobles alike as a matter of noble privilege. The dictionary enters Volhynia because the two things happened in one province within one generation: a Bible printed for a people who had never had one, and a doctrine printed that emptied the Bible of its Christ, and the second was protected by the same liberty as the first.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a magnate as a person of rank or great influence; collation as the comparing of copies; a privilege as a peculiar advantage enjoyed by a person or class; and satisfaction as that which fully answers a claim.

expand to see more

MAGNATE, n. A person of rank; a grandee or noble; a man of great power or influence.

COLLATION, n. The act of comparing one thing with another, as copies of a book or manuscript.

PRIVILEGE, n. A particular and peculiar benefit or advantage enjoyed by a person, company or society, beyond the common advantages of other citizens.

SATISFACTION, n. That which satisfies; payment; atonement for a crime; the payment of a debt or a penalty.

PRESS, n. A machine for printing; the art or business of printing and publishing.

Modern Corruption

Ruthenian province of the commonwealth where Prince Ostrogski printed the first complete Slavonic Bible in 1581 and the Polish Brethren were sheltered by noble privilege.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is antitrinitarianism, and Volhynia is where it enjoyed the most comfortable protection it ever had. The Polish Brethren taught that the Son is not God and that the cross is an example rather than a satisfaction, and they taught it under the Warsaw Confederation of 1573 with great nobles as patrons. The dictionary names the doctrine for what it is and names also what made it possible: a liberty held as the private right of a landowner, in which a congregation's doctrine depended on which lord owned the village. “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) is the test, and a patron's pleasure is not it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture given to a people in their own speech is the instrument that corrects them, which is why the Ostrog press was a greater service to Volhynia than any nobleman's protection. “The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul” (Psa 19:7) is the ground of every such labour. The Ostrog Bible also answers the objection that the eastern church had no translators: it had one magnate who paid for it, and the men of Pentecost heard “in our tongues the wonderful works of God” (Act 2:11), which is the warrant he worked on.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew torah (H8451), law, instruction; Hebrew tamim (H8549), perfect, complete; Greek glossa (G1100), a tongue.

expand to see more

Hebrew torah (H8451) — law, instruction, that which is taught; “The law of the LORD is perfect”, Psalm 19:7.

Hebrew tamim (H8549) — complete, whole, without blemish; “The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul”, Psalm 19:7.

Hebrew edah (H5715) — a testimony, an attested witness; “the testimony of the LORD is sure”, Psalm 19:7.

Greek glossa (G1100) — a tongue, and so a language; “we do hear them speak in our tongues”, Acts 2:11.

Greek krateo (G2902) — to hold fast, to retain; “hold that fast which thou hast”, Revelation 3:11.

Usage

"“The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul” (Psa 19:7) — the Ostrog Bible printed in 1581."

"“we do hear them speak in our tongues” (Act 2:11) — a Slavonic Bible for a people who had never had one printed."

"“To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — the Polish Brethren sheltered by noble privilege after 1573."
